templates.name: Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Specify or identify a single fact

items.subtype: Overview of a trade (two-way exchange over centuries)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Tea Horse Road was a network of footpaths connecting southwestern China and Tibet.
• Beginning in the eleventh century, Chinese officials exchanged tea for Tibetan horses, which the imperial cavalry required.
• Tibetans drank tea churned with butter and salt, prizing it as a supplement to a diet with few vegetables.
• Compressed into bricks, the tea was transported across steep passes by porters and mule caravans.
• The trade persisted until the 1950s, when highways rendered the footpaths obsolete.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the trade conducted along the Tea Horse Road. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: From the eleventh century until the 1950s, Chinese officials traded horses for Tibetan tea, which porters and mule caravans transported across steep passes as compressed bricks.
Compressed into bricks, tea from southwestern China was carried into Tibet over steep passes by porters and mule caravans.
For roughly nine centuries, until highways replaced the footpaths, China sent bricks of tea into Tibet and received horses for its cavalry in return.
Starting in the eleventh century, Tibet traded horses to China for tea, which Chinese officials prized as a supplement to a diet with few vegetables; the exchange lasted until the 1950s.
items.explanation: An overview must cover the whole trade: what went in each direction, why, and over what span of time. Choice C says that China sent tea into Tibet and received horses for its cavalry, and it covers the span from the eleventh century to the 1950s, when highways replaced the footpaths.

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: direction of the exchange reversed)
A.why_wrong: It spans the whole period but reverses the exchange. The notes say Chinese officials gave tea for Tibetan horses, not horses for Tibetan tea.

B.recipe: PART (how the tea was carried only)
B.why_wrong: It describes how tea was carried into Tibet but leaves out the horses, the exchange itself and its time span, so it is not an overview of the trade.

D.why_wrong: It gives the exchange and its time span, but it says Chinese officials prized tea as a supplement to their diet. According to the notes, it was Tibetans who prized tea that way; China wanted horses for its imperial cavalry.

items.notes: Subject: history (trade, China and Tibet). General knowledge, no named people. Band 7 per section 5: two goal-shaped FALSE options (A reverses who gave what, D swaps tea for the butter and salt of bullet 3) and one PART; the key compresses bullets 2 and 5 into a derived span (roughly nine centuries) and drops the dates. No bullet states the overview. Review: D was killed at once by the road's own name (butter and salt as trade goods), so it now swaps who prized the tea (bullet 3), and B became a transport-only PART so it no longer states the true version beside D; the key no longer copies bullet 2's "which the imperial cavalry required".

fixes: D hardened: was killed by the road name (butter and salt as goods); now swaps who prized the tea (bullet 3)
B changed to a transport-only PART so it no longer states the true version of D beside it
key paraphrased so it no longer copies bullet 2 ("which the imperial cavalry required")

band7.why: Two goal-shaped FALSE options that need a bullet check: A reverses who gave what, D gives the right exchange and span but swaps who prized the tea (bullet 3); B is PART. The key derives the span (roughly nine centuries), drops the dates and paraphrases. Neither FALSE option is the key's shape plus one figure. Notes register 23% rare, 5.31 chars per word.

items.subtype: Summarize two findings (numbers misattached in distractors)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Birds frequently fail to perceive glass, and window collisions kill huge numbers of them each year.
• Ecologist Corinne Vasseur and colleagues applied dot-printed adhesive film to the windows of an Ontario university building.
• Over the next two autumns, they recovered 84% fewer bird carcasses beneath the windows than in the two preceding autumns.
• When surveyed, 71% of the building’s occupants said the dots did not bother them.
• The researchers next intend to evaluate more widely spaced dots.
items.stem: The student wants to summarize the findings of Vasseur’s study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After Vasseur’s team covered a building’s windows with dotted film, far fewer dead birds were found below them, and most occupants did not mind the dots.
Vasseur and colleagues found that dotted film reduced the number of bird carcasses beneath a building’s windows by 71% and that 84% of the building’s occupants did not mind the dots.
Vasseur’s team recovered 84% fewer bird carcasses beneath the film-covered windows than beneath the building’s untreated windows, and most occupants said the dots did not bother them.
Having tested dotted film on an Ontario university building, Vasseur’s team next intends to find out whether more widely spaced dots would also prevent collisions.
items.explanation: The study had two findings: far fewer dead birds were found beneath the treated windows than before the film was added, and most of the building’s occupants were not bothered by the dots. Choice A presents both findings accurately without the figures.

B.why_wrong: It reports both findings but swaps the numbers: carcasses fell by 84%, and 71% of occupants said the dots did not bother them.

C.why_wrong: The 84% drop compares the two autumns after the film was applied with the two autumns before. The notes say the film went on the building’s windows and mention no untreated windows.

D.recipe: OG (the team’s next step, not its findings)
D.why_wrong: It describes what the team intends to test next, not what the study found.

items.notes: Subject: science (ornithology, conservation). Invented researcher (name searched: no ecologist of that name). Band 7 per section 5 (STUDY): present findings with two numeric findings; key drops the numbers; B misattaches both figures, C changes the comparison base (before and after, not treated and untreated). No aim or method goal.

fixes: key paraphrased away from bullet 3 ("bird carcasses ... recovered beneath")

band7.why: Matches official 5645f119: two numeric findings, the key drops the numbers, B swaps both figures, C keeps the 84% but changes the comparison base (untreated windows, not the preceding autumns), D is OG. The key carries no figures, so neither B nor C is the key plus one changed figure. Notes register 19% rare, 5.29 chars per word.

items.subtype: Introduce a book to an audience familiar with a movement
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Négritude was a literary movement founded in Paris during the 1930s by French-speaking Black intellectuals.
• Its founders, including Aimé Césaire, celebrated African and Caribbean cultural traditions in poetry and essays.
• In 2020, historian Josiane Bellegarde published A Salon in Clamart, about the Martinican sisters Paulette and Jane Nardal.
• Bellegarde maintains that the salon the Nardals hosted near Paris around 1930 nurtured ideas fundamental to Négritude.
• The book also covers Paulette’s later activism in Martinique.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce Bellegarde’s book to an audience already familiar with Négritude. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A Salon in Clamart, by historian Josiane Bellegarde, argues that the Nardal sisters’ salon shaped Négritude, the movement in which French-speaking Black intellectuals celebrated African and Caribbean cultures.
Négritude, a movement founded in Paris during the 1930s, counted Aimé Césaire among the intellectuals who celebrated African and Caribbean cultures in poetry and essays.
In A Salon in Clamart, historian Josiane Bellegarde covers the activism that Paulette Nardal later pursued in Martinique.
In A Salon in Clamart (2020), historian Josiane Bellegarde contends that the Nardal sisters’ salon near Paris helped nurture some of Négritude’s central ideas.
items.explanation: An audience that already knows Négritude needs to learn what the book is and what it argues, not what the movement was. Choice D names the book, its author and year, and its argument about the Nardal sisters’ salon, and it uses the term Négritude without explaining it.

A.recipe: AUD (complete, but re-explains the familiar movement)
A.why_wrong: It introduces the book and its argument but then explains what Négritude was, which this audience already knows.

B.recipe: OG (about the movement, not the book)
B.why_wrong: It describes Négritude and one of its founders and never mentions Bellegarde’s book.

C.recipe: PART (a secondary thread presented as the book’s subject)
C.why_wrong: It mentions only the part of the book about Paulette Nardal’s later activism and leaves out its main argument about the salon and Négritude.

items.notes: Subject: arts and literature (history of a literary movement). Invented historian and title (both searched: no such historian, no such book). The Nardal sisters, their salon near Paris (Clamart) and their link to Négritude are real; the book’s argument matches the established scholarly view. Strong band 6 (AUD_FAM has no band-7 officials): A is complete apart from the redefinition, the 2.1 D trap.

band7.why: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items; a strong band 6 like 39ccb463 (A complete apart from re-explaining Négritude, B OG, C PART).

items.subtype: Explanation plus example (which plant is the nurse)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A nurse plant is one whose shelter enhances the survival of seedlings belonging to other species.
• Young saguaro cacti grow slowly and are vulnerable to extreme heat and frost.
• In the Sonoran Desert, saguaros frequently germinate beneath palo verde trees.
• The trees’ canopies shade the seedlings during summer and keep them warm on cold nights.
• A mature saguaro may later compete with its palo verde for groundwater, sometimes contributing to the tree’s death.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of a nurse plant. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Nurse plants enhance the survival of seedlings belonging to other species, as the saguaro does when it shelters young palo verde trees from extreme heat and frost.
A nurse plant protects other species’ young; the palo verde, for instance, shields growing saguaros from summer heat and nighttime cold.
Young saguaros, which are vulnerable to extreme heat and frost, frequently germinate beneath palo verde trees in the Sonoran Desert.
A nurse plant shelters seedlings that will eventually replace it, as when a mature saguaro outcompetes the palo verde it germinated beneath.
items.explanation: Choice B explains what a nurse plant does (it protects the young of other species) and gives an example: the palo verde, whose canopy keeps young saguaros from overheating in summer and from freezing on cold nights.

A.why_wrong: It reverses the roles. The notes say young saguaros germinate beneath palo verde trees, so the palo verde is the nurse plant, not the saguaro.

C.why_wrong: It describes young saguaros growing under palo verde trees but never explains what a nurse plant is.

D.why_wrong: It defines a nurse plant as one whose seedlings replace it. The notes define it by the shelter it gives and say only that a mature saguaro may compete with its palo verde.

items.notes: Subject: science (desert ecology). General knowledge, no named people. Plan cell was band 7, but EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items (band7 file section 1), so written as strong band 6 on ec03f090 (PART, FALSE, FALSE). No bullet names the palo verde a nurse plant; the student links the definition to bullets 3 and 4.

band7.why: EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items; a strong band 6 on ec03f090 (two goal-shaped FALSE: roles reversed, wrong definition; one PART).

items.subtype: Difference on a named attribute (Unlike opener)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Africa’s elephants belong to two species that scientists long treated as one.
• Savanna elephants, the larger species, roam grasslands and open woodlands across much of the continent.
• Their tusks curve outward and forward.
• Forest elephants inhabit the dense rainforests of central and western Africa.
• Their tusks are straighter and point downward, which may help the animals move through thick vegetation.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the tusks of the two species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Savanna elephants roam grasslands and open woodlands, whereas forest elephants inhabit dense rainforests.
Forest elephants’ straighter, downward-pointing tusks may help them move through the thick vegetation of central and western Africa.
Though scientists long treated them as one species, savanna elephants and forest elephants have tusks that differ in shape.
Unlike savanna elephants, whose tusks curve outward and forward, forest elephants have straighter tusks that point downward.
items.explanation: Choice D sets the two kinds of tusk side by side: savanna elephants’ tusks curve outward and forward, while forest elephants’ tusks are straighter and point downward.

A.recipe: REL (a difference, but on the wrong attribute)
A.why_wrong: It contrasts the species’ habitats, not their tusks.

B.why_wrong: It describes forest elephants’ tusks but says nothing about savanna elephants’ tusks.

C.recipe: VAGUE (says the tusks differ without saying how)
C.why_wrong: It states that the tusks differ in shape but never says what the difference is.

items.notes: Subject: science (zoology). General knowledge. Goal names the attribute (tusks) so the habitat contrast in A is a wrong-dimension REL, not a second key.

items.subtype: Difference on a named attribute (surface), wrong-dimension trap
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Korean potters have developed several distinctive styles of stoneware.
• Celadon, which flourished during the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), is coated with a translucent blue-green glaze.
• Some celadon is inlaid with cranes and clouds.
• Buncheong ware gained popularity after the Joseon dynasty began in 1392.
• Before glazing, buncheong pieces are covered with white slip, a liquid clay, often brushed with loose patterns.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how the surface of buncheong ware differs from that of celadon. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Whereas celadon’s surface is a translucent blue-green glaze, buncheong ware is covered with white slip before it is glazed.
Celadon flourished under the Goryeo dynasty, which ended in 1392, while buncheong ware gained popularity after the Joseon dynasty began that year.
Buncheong pieces were covered with white slip, a liquid clay that potters often brushed with loose patterns.
Celadon and buncheong ware are both distinctive styles of stoneware developed by Korean potters.
items.explanation: The goal asks about surfaces. Choice A contrasts them directly: celadon has a translucent blue-green glaze, while buncheong ware is first covered with white slip.

B.recipe: REL (difference on the wrong attribute: time period)
B.why_wrong: It contrasts when the two styles were popular, not their surfaces.

C.why_wrong: It describes the surface of buncheong ware but never mentions celadon.

D.why_wrong: It states what the two styles have in common, not how they differ.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Korean ceramics). General knowledge. Two differences exist in the notes (period and surface); the goal names the surface, as 2.44 names the start of careers, so B is a wrong-dimension trap.

items.subtype: Contrast two methods (but-joined key)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A census is an official count of a country’s population.
• The United States conducts its census every ten years.
• It mails questionnaires to households and sends workers door-to-door to reach those that do not respond.
• Since 1990, Finland has compiled its census entirely from existing government records, such as population and tax registers.
• As a result, Finnish residents receive no census questionnaires.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how the United States and Finland gather census data. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A census, an official count of a country’s population, is conducted every ten years in the United States.
Although the United States and Finland both conduct censuses, the two countries collect their census information in quite different ways.
The United States gathers census data through questionnaires and door-to-door visits, but Finland relies solely on records its government already maintains.
Since 1990, Finland has compiled its census entirely from population and tax registers, so Finnish residents never receive census questionnaires.
items.explanation: Choice C gives each country’s method and joins them with “but”: the United States uses questionnaires and door-to-door visits, while Finland relies on records the government already holds.

A.why_wrong: It defines a census and says how often the US takes one; it says nothing about Finland.

B.recipe: VAGUE (says the methods differ without saying how)
B.why_wrong: It claims the two countries collect data differently but never describes either method.

D.why_wrong: It describes Finland’s method but not the US method.

items.notes: Subject: social science (government statistics). General knowledge (Finland’s register-based census since 1990; US decennial census with mail and nonresponse follow-up). Replaces a textbook economics pair swapped before writing.

items.subtype: Introduce a researcher to an audience unfamiliar with her field
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hind Ouazzani is a Moroccan paleontologist.
• She specializes in ichnology, the study of trace fossils.
• Trace fossils are preserved evidence of an organism’s activity, such as footprints, burrows, and nests, rather than its body.
• Ouazzani has documented more than 300 dinosaur footprints in Morocco’s High Atlas Mountains.
• Some tracks were left along the shoreline of an ancient lagoon.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce Ouazzani’s research to an audience unfamiliar with ichnology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: As an ichnologist, Ouazzani has documented more than 300 dinosaur footprints in Morocco’s High Atlas Mountains.

Moroccan paleontologist Hind Ouazzani studies trace fossils, the footprints and other signs that ancient animals left behind, and has documented more than 300 dinosaur tracks in the High Atlas Mountains.
Ichnology is the study of trace fossils, such as footprints, burrows, and nests, which preserve evidence of an organism’s activity rather than its body.
Some of the more than 300 dinosaur footprints in Morocco’s High Atlas Mountains were left along the shoreline of an ancient lagoon.
items.explanation: An audience new to ichnology needs to know who Ouazzani is and what her field studies. Choice B identifies her as a Moroccan paleontologist, explains trace fossils in plain terms, and then gives her research: more than 300 dinosaur tracks in the High Atlas Mountains.

A.recipe: AUD (uses the field’s term without explaining it)
A.why_wrong: It calls Ouazzani an ichnologist without explaining what ichnology is, which this audience does not know.

C.why_wrong: It explains ichnology but never mentions Ouazzani or her research.

D.why_wrong: It describes some of the footprints but does not introduce Ouazzani or explain her field.

items.notes: Subject: science (paleontology). Invented researcher (name searched; an earlier choice turned out to be a famous person’s name and was dropped). Real region; the documentation work is invented and attributed only to her.

fixes: key gloss turned from parentheses into an appositive; "over 300" to "more than 300"

items.subtype: Present a significance to an audience unfamiliar with a script
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cuneiform, a script of wedge-shaped marks, was used in ancient Mesopotamia for roughly 3,000 years.
• Knowledge of how to read it was later lost.
• Around 520 BCE, Persian king Darius I had an inscription carved into a cliff at Behistun, in Iran.
• It presents an identical text in three languages, all written in cuneiform.
• Transcribed in the 1830s and 1840s, it enabled scholars to decipher cuneiform.
items.stem: The student wants to present the significance of the Behistun Inscription to an audience unfamiliar with cuneiform. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Presenting one text in three languages, the Behistun Inscription let scholars decipher cuneiform, a long-unreadable Mesopotamian script of wedge-shaped marks.
Transcribed by scholars in the 1830s and 1840s, the Behistun Inscription enabled them to decipher cuneiform.
Around 520 BCE, Persian king Darius I had the Behistun Inscription carved into a cliff in Iran.
Cuneiform, a script of wedge-shaped marks, was used in ancient Mesopotamia for roughly 3,000 years before knowledge of how to read it was lost.
items.explanation: Choice A presents why the inscription matters (its three versions of one text let scholars decipher cuneiform) and explains cuneiform for readers who have never heard of it: a Mesopotamian script of wedge-shaped marks that had become unreadable.

B.why_wrong: It gives the inscription’s significance but never says what cuneiform is, which this audience does not know.

C.recipe: OG (when and by whom it was carved)
C.why_wrong: It says who had the inscription carved and where, not why it is significant.

D.why_wrong: It describes cuneiform but never mentions the Behistun Inscription.

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient Near East, decipherment). General knowledge. Like 2.35, the key pairs the significance with a gloss of the unfamiliar term; B is 2.35 C’s shape.

items.subtype: Emphasize accuracy (derived comparison)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Dresden Codex is one of only four Maya books that survived the Spanish conquest.
• It contains astronomical tables for tracking the planet Venus.
• These tables assume a 584-day cycle, the time Venus takes to return to the same position relative to the Sun.
• Modern measurements put the cycle’s average length at 583.92 days.
• The codex is now held in Dresden, Germany.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the accuracy of the Venus cycle used in the Dresden Codex. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Dresden Codex, which contains astronomical tables for tracking Venus, is one of only four Maya books that survived the Spanish conquest.
The Venus tables in the Dresden Codex assume a 584-day cycle, the time the planet takes to return to the same position relative to the Sun.
The Dresden Codex’s 584-day Venus cycle differs by less than a tenth of a day from the 583.92-day average established by modern measurements.
Now held in Dresden, Germany, the codex contains tables that track the movements of Venus.
items.explanation: Accuracy is shown by comparison with a known value. Choice C sets the codex’s 584 days beside the modern figure of 583.92 days and points out that they differ by less than a tenth of a day.

A.why_wrong: It stresses how rare the codex is, not how accurate its Venus cycle is.

B.why_wrong: It gives the codex’s 584-day cycle but never compares it with the modern measurement, so it does not show accuracy.

D.why_wrong: It says where the codex is kept and what it contains, not how accurate it is.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (Maya astronomy). General knowledge (four surviving Maya codices; synodic period of Venus 583.92 days). The key derives “less than a tenth of a day” from two bullets; no bullet states the accuracy.

items.subtype: Explain why (cause linked across three bullets)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cryoconite is a dark mixture of windblown dust, soot, and microbes that collects on glacier surfaces.
• Dark materials absorb more of the Sun’s heat than the white ice around them.
• Gradually, clumps of cryoconite melt the ice beneath them, forming small, water-filled pits called cryoconite holes.
• These holes are usually a few centimeters to half a meter deep.
• Microbes in the holes remain active even at subfreezing temperatures.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why cryoconite holes form. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Cryoconite, a dark mixture of windblown dust, soot, and microbes, collects on glacier surfaces.
Being dark, cryoconite absorbs more of the Sun’s heat than the surrounding ice does, so it melts its way down into the glacier, leaving a hole.
Cryoconite holes are small, water-filled pits, usually a few centimeters to half a meter deep, found in glacier ice.
The microbes living in cryoconite holes remain active even when temperatures above the glacier are subfreezing.
items.explanation: Choice B links cause and effect: cryoconite is dark, so it absorbs more heat than the white ice around it, and that heat melts the ice beneath it, forming the hole.

A.why_wrong: It says what cryoconite is made of and where it is found, not why the holes form.

C.why_wrong: It describes the holes’ size and shape but not what causes them.

D.why_wrong: It describes the microbes in the holes, not how the holes come to exist.

items.notes: Subject: science (glaciology). General knowledge. Like 2.31, the cause sits in one bullet (2) and the effect in another (3); only the key joins them.

items.subtype: Explain why (chain of three bullets)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Katabatic winds are winds propelled down a slope by gravity.
• Over the Antarctic ice sheet, air touching the frigid surface loses heat and grows colder than the surrounding air.
• Colder air is denser, and therefore heavier, than warmer air.
• The ice sheet slopes down from the elevated interior toward the coast.
• Along portions of the coast, katabatic winds can exceed 150 kilometers per hour.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why katabatic winds blow toward Antarctica’s coast. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Along portions of Antarctica’s coast, katabatic winds can exceed 150 kilometers per hour.
Air touching the Antarctic ice sheet loses heat, growing colder and therefore denser and heavier than the surrounding air.
Katabatic winds are winds that are propelled down a slope by the force of gravity.
Chilled by the ice sheet, the air above it grows heavier than warmer air, so gravity pulls it down the sheet’s slope toward the coast.
items.explanation: Choice D gives the whole chain: the ice chills the air above it, cold air is heavier, and gravity pulls that heavy air down the ice sheet, which slopes from the interior to the coast.

A.why_wrong: It says how fast the winds can blow, not why they blow toward the coast.

B.recipe: PART (the cooling without the downhill flow)
B.why_wrong: It explains why the air becomes dense but not why that air moves toward the coast.

C.why_wrong: It defines katabatic winds in general but says nothing about Antarctica’s ice sheet or its slope.

items.notes: Subject: science (meteorology). General knowledge. Key derives the flow direction from bullets 2 to 4; B carries the first half of the chain only.

items.subtype: Similarity of two plants (shared pollinator)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Numerous flowering plants depend on animals to transfer pollen between flowers.
• The baobab, a tree of the African savanna, is recognizable by its massive, swollen trunk.
• Its large white flowers, which open at night, are pollinated primarily by fruit bats.
• The durian is a Southeast Asian tree known for its spiky, pungent fruit.
• Its flowers are pollinated primarily by nectar-feeding bats.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the baobab and the durian. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The baobab and the durian, though native to different continents, both rely primarily on bats for pollination.
The baobab is recognizable by its massive, swollen trunk, whereas the durian is known for its spiky, pungent fruit.
The baobab’s large white flowers, which open at night, are pollinated primarily by fruit bats.
Like numerous other flowering plants, the durian depends on animals to transfer pollen between its flowers.
items.explanation: Choice A names both trees and the trait they share: each is pollinated primarily by bats.

B.why_wrong: It contrasts the trees’ best-known features instead of pointing to something they share.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the baobab is pollinated but never mentions the durian.

D.recipe: OG (a general fact, not the two trees)
D.why_wrong: It compares the durian with flowering plants in general, not with the baobab.

items.notes: Subject: science (botany, pollination). General knowledge. One shared trait only: night opening is given for the baobab alone, so no second similarity exists.

items.subtype: Order in time (two maps)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Fifteenth-century mapmakers working at opposite ends of Eurasia produced two notable world maps.
• Officials of Korea’s royal court created the Kangnido in 1402.
• It exaggerates Korea’s size but includes a recognizable outline of Africa.
• The Fra Mauro map was completed in Venice around 1450.
• Measuring nearly two meters across, it is oriented with south at the top.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the order in which the two maps were made. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Kangnido includes a recognizable outline of Africa, while the Fra Mauro map is oriented with south at the top.
The Kangnido was created in Korea about half a century before the Fra Mauro map was completed in Venice.
Completed around 1450, the Fra Mauro map preceded Korea’s Kangnido by several decades.
Both the Kangnido and the Fra Mauro map are world maps that were produced in the fifteenth century.
items.explanation: The Kangnido dates from 1402 and the Fra Mauro map from around 1450. Choice B states that order, placing the Kangnido about fifty years earlier.

A.why_wrong: It contrasts what the two maps show, not when they were made.

C.why_wrong: It puts the Fra Mauro map first, but the notes date the Kangnido to 1402, about fifty years earlier.

D.why_wrong: It says both maps come from the same century but not which came first.

items.notes: Subject: history (cartography). General knowledge. Key drops the raw dates and states the interval, as 2.44 does; C is 2.27 C’s reversal.

items.subtype: Provide an example (beside a neighboring concept)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Geographers define an exclave as part of a country that foreign territory separates from the rest of it.
• An enclave is a territory entirely surrounded by a single other country.
• San Marino, surrounded by Italy, is an enclave.
• Oecusse, a coastal region on the island of Timor, is an exclave of Timor-Leste.
• Indonesian territory separates it from the rest of the country.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an example of an exclave. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: San Marino, which is surrounded by Italy, is an example of an enclave.
An exclave is separated from the rest of its country by foreign territory, whereas an enclave is entirely surrounded by a single country.
Oecusse, a region of Timor-Leste separated from the rest of the country by Indonesian territory, is one example of an exclave.
Oecusse is a coastal region on the island of Timor.
items.explanation: Choice C names a specific exclave, Oecusse, and shows why it qualifies: Indonesian territory cuts it off from the rest of Timor-Leste.

A.recipe: OG (an example of the other concept)
A.why_wrong: It gives an example of an enclave, not an exclave.

B.why_wrong: It contrasts the two terms but names no specific exclave.

D.recipe: PART (the instance without the link to the concept)
D.why_wrong: It says where Oecusse is but not that it is an exclave or why.

items.notes: Subject: social science (political geography). General knowledge. A is the 2.43 move: an example of the neighboring concept.

items.subtype: Present the aim and method
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Countdown signals show pedestrians how many seconds remain before the signal changes.
• Transportation researcher Daniela Arancibia wanted to learn whether such signals reduce the number of people still crossing when the signal changes.
• Her team filmed more than 4,000 crossings at eight intersections in Santiago, Chile.
• They recorded crossings both before and after countdown signals were installed.
• Late crossings fell by about a third once the signals were in use.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim and method of Arancibia’s study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After countdown signals were installed at eight intersections in Santiago, Chile, late crossings fell by about a third.
Arancibia wanted to learn whether countdown signals, which show pedestrians how many seconds remain, reduce late crossings.
Arancibia’s team filmed more than 4,000 pedestrian crossings at eight intersections in Santiago, Chile.
To learn whether countdown signals reduce late crossings, Arancibia’s team filmed crossings at eight Santiago intersections before and after the signals were installed.
items.explanation: The aim was to learn whether countdown signals cut late crossings; the method was to film crossings at eight intersections before and after the signals went in. Choice D gives both.

A.recipe: OG (the result, not the aim or method)
A.why_wrong: It reports what the study found rather than what it set out to learn and how.

B.why_wrong: It gives the aim but not how the team carried out the study.

C.why_wrong: It describes the filming but not the aim, and it leaves out the before-and-after comparison.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban transportation). Invented researcher (name searched: no such transportation researcher) and invented study in a real city.

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience familiar with its technique
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In cloisonné, thin metal wires are attached to an object’s surface to create small compartments.
• These are filled with enamel, a colored glass paste, before the object is fired.
• Michiko Arakawa is a Japanese artist who has practiced cloisonné since the 1990s.
• Her 2018 vase Night Crossing depicts cranes migrating across a dark-blue sky.
• Their wings are outlined in silver wire.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Night Crossing to an audience already familiar with cloisonné. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Night Crossing is a 2018 cloisonné vase, meaning that metal wires attached to its surface form compartments filled with colored enamel.
Arakawa’s 2018 cloisonné vase Night Crossing depicts cranes, their wings outlined in silver wire, migrating across a dark-blue sky.
Michiko Arakawa, a Japanese artist who attaches thin wires to her works’ surfaces and fills the resulting compartments with enamel, has practiced cloisonné since the 1990s.
Japanese artist Michiko Arakawa created the vase Night Crossing in 2018.
items.explanation: An audience that knows cloisonné needs only the details of this vase. Choice B names the vase as cloisonné without explaining the technique and describes what it shows (cranes crossing a dark-blue sky) and how they are drawn (wings outlined in silver wire).

A.why_wrong: It spends the sentence explaining how cloisonné works, which this audience already knows, and says nothing about what the vase shows.

C.recipe: AUD (explains the technique and describes the artist, not the vase)
C.why_wrong: It explains cloisonné again and introduces Arakawa but never describes Night Crossing.

D.recipe: OG (identifies the work without describing it)
D.why_wrong: It says who made the vase and when but not what it looks like.

items.notes: Subject: arts (enamelwork). Invented artist and work (name searched: no cloisonné artist of that name).

fixes: key names the vase as cloisonné without explaining it, as official 2.18 does with "leporello"

items.subtype: Make a generalization (a class one level up)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Paper, invented in China, required many centuries to spread to other regions.
• In early China, texts were inscribed on bamboo strips bound together with cord.
• Across southern and southeastern Asia, scribes wrote on dried palm leaves.
• In the medieval Russian city of Novgorod, residents scratched messages into birch bark.
• One surviving fragment contains drawings by a boy named Onfim from the 1200s.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about what people wrote on where paper was not yet available. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Examples of writing surfaces include bamboo strips in early China and dried palm leaves across southern and southeastern Asia.
In medieval Novgorod, a boy named Onfim made drawings on a fragment of birch bark that still survives.
Before paper reached them, people in many regions wrote on materials that came from plants.
Paper required many centuries to spread from China, where it was invented, to other regions.
items.explanation: A generalization makes a claim about a whole group. Bamboo, palm leaves, and birch bark all come from plants, so Choice C generalizes that, where people lacked paper, they wrote on plant materials.

A.why_wrong: It lists two examples but makes no broader claim about them.

B.why_wrong: It describes a single surviving fragment of birch bark, not a pattern.

D.recipe: OG (a generalization about the wrong subject)
D.why_wrong: It makes a claim about how paper spread, not about what people wrote on without it.

items.notes: Subject: history (writing materials). General knowledge (Novgorod birch-bark letters, Onfim’s drawings). The class “materials that came from plants” is derived; no bullet states it.

fixes: key no longer opens with the stem's exact phrase

items.subtype: Use a quotation to explain how something works
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Seed libraries lend seeds rather than books.
• Borrowers cultivate the seeds at home, allow some plants to produce seeds, and return a portion of those seeds.
• In 2013, librarian Ruth Engstrom established a seed library at her Vermont town’s public library.
• Describing how the collection evolves, she remarked, “Every season, the seeds we get back are better adapted to the soil and climate right here.”
• She also observed, “Gardeners who had never visited the library now arrive every spring.”
items.stem: The student wants to explain how the seed library’s collection improves over time, using a quotation from Engstrom. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Borrowers return seeds from plants they grew at home, so, as Engstrom remarked, “Every season, the seeds we get back are better adapted to the soil and climate right here.”
According to Engstrom, the seeds that borrowers return grow increasingly suited to local conditions each season.
Engstrom observed that the seed library has attracted new patrons: “Gardeners who had never visited the library now arrive every spring.”
Seed libraries, such as the one Engstrom established in her Vermont town in 2013, lend seeds rather than books, and borrowers return a portion of the seeds their plants produce.
items.explanation: Choice A explains the mechanism (borrowers return seeds from plants they grew at home) and quotes Engstrom’s words about the result: each season the returned seeds are better adapted to local soil and climate.

B.why_wrong: It explains the improvement but uses no quotation from Engstrom, which the goal requires.

C.why_wrong: It quotes Engstrom, but the quotation is about the library’s new visitors, not about how the collection improves.

D.recipe: OG (how a seed library works, no improvement, no quotation)
D.why_wrong: It describes how seed libraries lend seeds but neither explains the improvement nor quotes Engstrom.

items.notes: Subject: social science (libraries, community gardening). Invented librarian and invented quotations (name searched: no seed librarian of that name). Real concept.

items.subtype: Identify who designed a building
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Lotus Temple is a house of worship in New Delhi, India.
• Completed in 1986, it welcomes worshippers of every religion.
• It was designed by Iranian-born architect Fariborz Sahba.
• Its 27 white marble “petals” are arranged in clusters of three.
• The temple attracts millions of visitors annually.
items.stem: The student wants to identify the architect of the Lotus Temple. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Completed in 1986, the Lotus Temple in New Delhi welcomes worshippers of every religion.
The Lotus Temple’s 27 white marble “petals” are arranged in clusters of three.
New Delhi’s Lotus Temple, a house of worship, attracts millions of visitors annually.
The Lotus Temple in New Delhi was designed by Iranian-born architect Fariborz Sahba.
items.explanation: The goal asks who designed the building. Choice D names the architect, Fariborz Sahba.

A.why_wrong: It gives when the temple was completed and whom it welcomes, not who designed it.

B.why_wrong: It describes the temple’s petals but does not name the architect.

C.why_wrong: It says how many people visit, not who designed the temple.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture). General knowledge (Fariborz Sahba, completed 1986, 27 petals in clusters of three).

items.subtype: Similarity of two instruments (one shared feature)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The oud is a stringed instrument played across the Middle East and North Africa.
• Its body resembles a pear sliced lengthwise in half.
• Its neck has no frets, the raised ridges marking individual notes.
• The pipa is a stringed instrument traditionally played in China.
• Its body is pear-shaped, and frets run along its neck and soundboard.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the oud and the pipa. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The oud, which is played across the Middle East and North Africa, has a body resembling a pear sliced in half.
The oud and the pipa both have pear-shaped bodies.
The oud’s neck has no frets, whereas the pipa has frets along its neck and soundboard.
The pipa, a stringed instrument traditionally played in China, has frets running along its neck and soundboard.
items.explanation: Choice B names both instruments and a feature they share: a pear-shaped body.

A.why_wrong: It describes the oud’s body but never mentions the pipa.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts the instruments’ frets instead of pointing to something they share.

D.why_wrong: It describes the pipa but never mentions the oud.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music, instruments). General knowledge. No option states the other shared trait (both are stringed instruments), so only the key gives a similarity.

items.subtype: Describe a layout
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Caravanserais were inns built along trade routes across Central Asia, Persia, and the Middle East.
• They gave merchants, pilgrims, and their animals a safe place to stay overnight.
• A typical caravanserai was built around a large open courtyard.
• Rooms for travelers lined all four sides of the courtyard.
• A single gateway, wide enough for loaded camels, was the only entrance.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the layout of a typical caravanserai. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Caravanserais gave merchants, pilgrims, and their animals a safe place to stay overnight.
Caravanserais were inns built along trade routes across Central Asia, Persia, and the Middle East.
A typical caravanserai had rooms for travelers on all four sides of a large open courtyard, entered through a single gateway.
The gateway of a caravanserai was wide enough for loaded camels to pass through.
items.explanation: Choice C puts the layout together: a large open courtyard, rooms on all four sides, and one gateway as the entrance.

A.why_wrong: It explains what caravanserais were for, not how they were laid out.

B.why_wrong: It says where caravanserais were built, not how they were arranged.

D.why_wrong: It describes the gateway only and leaves out the courtyard and rooms.

items.notes: Subject: history (architecture of trade routes). General knowledge.

items.subtype: Define a term and give an example
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A glacial erratic is a boulder transported by a glacier far from its place of origin and deposited when the ice melted.
• The Okotoks Erratic rests on the prairie near Okotoks, Alberta, in Canada.
• It weighs about 16,500 tons and is split into two main pieces.
• Its rock matches bedrock near Jasper, Alberta, approximately 500 kilometers away.
items.stem: The student wants to provide a definition and an example of a glacial erratic. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A glacial erratic, such as the Okotoks Erratic in Alberta, is a boulder that a glacier transported far from its place of origin.
The Okotoks Erratic, which weighs about 16,500 tons and is split into two main pieces, rests on the prairie near Okotoks, Alberta.
Glaciers can transport boulders far from their places of origin, depositing them when the ice melts.
The rock of the Okotoks Erratic matches bedrock near Jasper, Alberta, approximately 500 kilometers away.
items.explanation: Choice A does both jobs: it defines a glacial erratic (a boulder a glacier carried far from where it formed) and names one, the Okotoks Erratic.

B.why_wrong: It describes the Okotoks Erratic but never says what a glacial erratic is.

C.recipe: VAGUE (the idea without the term or an example)
C.why_wrong: It describes what glaciers can do but never uses the term or gives an example.

D.why_wrong: It gives a fact about the boulder’s rock but defines nothing.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology). General knowledge (Big Rock, about 16,500 tonnes, from the Jasper area).
